decision: Jenisha S. Likansis v. Walmart Inc., et al., C.A. No. 2025-1455-DG (Del. Ch. Oct. 13, 2026) (Gibbs, M.)

summary.core_legal_issue: Whether a former Walmart Connect employee who held the added title "Chief of Staff" to the division's head was entitled to mandatory advancement under Walmart Inc.'s Bylaws (art. VI, § 2(a)), either as an "officer of the Corporation" or as a person serving "at the request of the Corporation" as an officer of "another enterprise" (Walmart Connect, an internal division, or Wal-Mart.com USA, LLC), where officer status under each governing instrument turns on appointment by a designated body rather than on the role's officer-like functions.
summary.standard_of_review: Ct. Ch. R. 56 summary judgment on cross-motions, each examined separately; Defendants bore the burden on both motions under Bylaws art. VI, § 5(d).
key_facts_and_concessions: Plaintiff's offer letter named Wal-Mart.com USA, LLC ("Walmart LLC"), a separate entity with its own Operating Agreement, as her employer; nothing shows her employing entity changed when she took the Chief of Staff title in January 2023.
Walmart Connect is an internal division of Walmart with no separate governing agreement or officers; both sides agree it is not a separate entity.

Plaintiff conceded she was appointed by Rich Lehrfeld, the "CEO/General Manager" of Walmart Connect, and not by Walmart's Board or CEO; Walmart's SEC filings show Lehrfeld was not Walmart's CEO or an executive officer.
Walmart concedes Plaintiff is eligible for permissive advancement, which it contends is in its sole discretion; it offered her defense counsel, which she declined as conflicted (fn. 12-13).

Walmart LLC's officers must be elected by "the Manager," a defined term (Fernando Madeira); counsel's post-argument sworn declaration and written consents established that neither Lehrfeld nor Ms. Bolles was a manager of Walmart LLC (fn. 78).
Plaintiff was dismissed with prejudice from the underlying New Jersey action on June 23, 2026, and has moved there for reconsideration and vacatur (fn. 21).
arguments_rejected_or_waived: Bylaws ambiguity: rejected. The open-ended "such other officers" language does not make the Bylaws ambiguous; they plainly require appointment by the Board or the CEO, so the functional character of Plaintiff's role is beside the point.

Delegation of appointment authority to Lehrfeld under Bylaws art. IV, § 11: waived because first raised in the reply brief; it differs substantively from the opening-brief argument and the Bylaws were available from the outset (fn. 55 notes Defendants wrongly said the Bylaws provide no delegation mechanism).

Walmart LLC officer theory: Defendants' waiver argument rejected because Plaintiff first obtained the Operating Agreement with Defendants' reply brief (fn. 29); rejected on the merits because she was not elected by the Manager.

"At the request of" Walmart (Walmart Connect theory): not reached in the text, but fn. 65 finds Plaintiff offered no evidence, since appointment by unspecified "leadership" is conclusory and Lehrfeld is not "Walmart."
Operating Agreement § 3.7 as a bar to summary judgment: rejected; it incorporates Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.08, which mandates indemnification only for members and managers.
Mandatory advancement under 8 Del. C. § 145: not considered, because § 145 advancement is purely permissive (fn. 22).
Plaintiff's objection to the post-argument submission: overruled; the materials responded to the Court's questions (fn. 20).

authorities_cited.authority: Bylaws art. VI, § 2(a) and art. IV, §§ 1, 2, 11
authorities_cited.proposition: Mandatory advancement extends to officers of the Corporation and those serving at its request as officers of another enterprise; officers are elected by the Board or, for limited categories, the CEO; § 11 permits the Board to delegate an officer's powers.
Officers beyond those named must be elected by "the Manager"; § 3.7 indemnifies officers and employees only to the extent California law permits.
Statutory advancement is purely permissive, so only contractual mandatory advancement rights were at issue.

authorities_cited.authority: Gilbert v. Unisys Corp., 2024 WL 3789952 (Del. Ch. Aug. 13, 2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: Section 145 advancement is permissive; "another enterprise" may lack formal legal existence, employees, payroll or the ability to confer officer titles, so a division can arguably qualify.

authorities_cited.authority: Tafeen v. Homestore, Inc., 2004 WL 556733 (Del. Ch. Mar. 22, 2004)
authorities_cited.proposition: Unambiguous bylaws are construed as written.

authorities_cited.authority: Jung v. El Tinieblo Int'l, Inc., 2022 WL 16557663 (Del. Ch. Oct. 31, 2022)
authorities_cited.proposition: An argument not raised in the opening brief is generally waived; waiver turns on fairness, and a reply argument that differs substantively and materially from the opening brief may be deemed waived.

authorities_cited.authority: McLaughlin v. Dover Downs, Inc., 2009 WL 1474707 (Del. 2009) (TABLE)
authorities_cited.proposition: Conclusory assertions without probative value do not create a genuine issue of material fact.
An LLC must indemnify members and managers but may indemnify officers, employees and agents.

authorities_cited.authority: Sassano v. CIBC World Mkts. Corp., 948 A.2d 453 (Del. Ch. 2008)
authorities_cited.proposition: Cited through Gilbert for the breadth of "another enterprise."

authorities_cited.authority: Senior Tour Players 207 Mgmt. Co. LLC v. Golftown 207 Hldg. Co., LLC, 853 A.2d 124 (Del. Ch. 2004)
authorities_cited.proposition: Summary judgment suits advancement disputes because they turn on the governing instruments and the underlying pleadings.

authorities_cited.authority: Bernstein v. TractManager, Inc., 953 A.2d 1003 (Del. Ch. 2007)
authorities_cited.proposition: Cross-motions do not change the summary judgment standard; each is examined separately.

authorities_cited.authority: Franklin Balance Sheet Inv. Fund v. Crowley, 2006 WL 3095952 (Del. Ch. Oct. 19, 2006)
authorities_cited.proposition: A movant must present all grounds and arguments in its opening brief.
Officer titles and managers' offices derive from the bylaws or LLC agreement; cited for the point that a division has no officers in the statutory sense.
The Court gave the post-argument declaration and documents the weight and credibility they deserved.
The parties consented to final adjudication by a Magistrate in Chancery, so the report issues as an opinion subject to ordinary appellate review.

summary.holding: Plaintiff's motion for summary judgment denied; Walmart's cross-motion granted. Plaintiff was not an officer of Walmart because the Bylaws require appointment by the Board or CEO and she was appointed by Lehrfeld, who was neither. Assuming arguendo that Walmart Connect is "another enterprise," the same appointment rule governs its officers, so that theory fails too. She was not an officer of Walmart LLC because its officers must be elected by the Manager, which Lehrfeld was not. Because she was an officer of none of the three, the Court did not reach whether she served "at the request of" Walmart.
summary.brief_summary: A former Walmart Connect Chief of Staff, appearing pro se after being named in a New Jersey discrimination suit, sought mandatory advancement from Walmart Inc. under its Bylaws, and the parties cross-moved for summary judgment before a Magistrate in Chancery sitting by consent under 10 Del. C. § 350. The Court held that officer status under each governing instrument depends on appointment by the body that instrument designates (Walmart's Board or CEO, or the LLC's Manager), not on whether a role is officer-like, and that her admitted appointment by a division head defeated all three of her theories. Her delegation theory was waived as first raised in reply, while her Walmart LLC theory was heard because she obtained the Operating Agreement only with Walmart's reply brief.
summary.practical_takeaway: Claimants seeking mandatory advancement as officers should establish the formal appointment chain under the operative bylaws or LLC agreement, and raise any delegation or alternative-appointment theory in the opening brief; companies can defeat functional-officer claims with SEC filings and written manager consents even when they bear the burden.
